newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGB rally seen continuing despite meagre yield.
newsitem.headline: JGB rally seen continuing despite meagre yield.

text.p: Japanese government bonds (JGBs), the darling of domestic investors despite record-low yields, look set to keep rallying, and the benchmark yield may dip below two percent in the next few months, traders say.

Japanese investors, they add, are flocking to JGBs mainly because they have few palatable domestic alternatives, with Tokyo shares languishing and bank debentures looking too risky as worries mount about Japan's financial system.
"Investors are becoming more meticulous about the types of bonds they buy," said Hidenobu Furuhashi, a manager at Toyo Trust & Banking Co Ltd's trading department.
Japanese institutions also have plenty of money on hand to invest domestically, market sources said.

"Basically, there are still a lot of (financial) institutions which have excess funds, and I think some of that money will probably flow into the bond market," said Hideaki Matsutoya, senior vice-president at Lehman Brothers Japan Inc.

Furuhashi and Matsutoya noted that investors have been buying up JGBs with particular zest since the start of the new fiscal year on April 1, with city banks, life insurers and agricultural financial bodies among the more eager buyers.
Life insurers already held 24.61 trillion yen worth of JGBs as of the end of January.

Buyers were egged on by recent signs that Japan's monetary authorities would keep short-term interest rates at historic lows, especially after the latest "tankan" survey of business confidence showed most Japanese businesses were still pessimistic about the economic outlook going into the summer.

Demand for JGBs is likely to remain strong relative to supply throughout this fiscal year, said Toyo Trust's Furuhashi, due in part to a large redemption of JGBs coming up in June. The Bond Underwriters' Association of Japan said approximately 5.1 trillion yen worth of 10-year JGBs will reach maturity at that time.
Traders expect a large portion of the redeemed funds will be ploughed back into JGBs.
Against this background, Furuhashi predicted the key JGB yield may fall as low as 1.8 percent in the next few months.
The benchmark 182nd JGB yield stood at 2.150 percent as of 0045 GMT on Thursday.

Echoing this bullishness, Takashi Ueno, senior manager at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd's securities investment division, said the benchmark 182nd JGB yield may briefly fall below two percent in the April-June quarter.
But he was more cautious about the longer-term outlook, predicting that the rise in JGBs would probably be capped as the economic recovery picks up steam and the dollar keeps surging against the yen.
Such developments may spur the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates earlier than the market expects, he said.
Ueno added that moves by public funds, such as the Finance Ministry's Trust Fund Bureau, the Bank of Japan, the postal savings system and the Postal Life Insurance Bureau (Kampo), also bear watching.
Although these funds now play a huge role in the JGB market, the continued drop in yen interest rates has made some of them more cautious about buying JGBs.
"We cannot be too comfortable about parking funds in yen bonds with the yield repeatedly setting record lows," a Kampo official told Reuters earlier this month.
Kampo is the largest institutional investor in Japan with total assets of 97.22 trillion yen as of the end of February. Its holdings of JGBs totalled 35.04 trillion yen, or 36 percent of the total.
Ueno also pointed out, however, that Kampo's cautiousness has not dampened buying enthusiasm among other market players.
